posts.linkedin:
Today I'm releasing BioManager {version}, free and open source.

Most labs I know run on twenty spreadsheets, a whiteboard and paper cage cards. BioManager puts the mouse colony, zebrafish, fly and worm stocks, plasmids, samples, orders, reagents, antibodies, viruses, the calendar and a lab notebook in one app. You edit it like a spreadsheet, but underneath it is a real database: it knows which mouse is in which cage, when a litter needs weaning and which antibody is about to expire, and it tells you. And the records are connected: a sample knows the mouse it came from, and writing @mouse 16 in a notebook page links straight to that mouse.

It runs as a desktop app for one person (macOS, Windows, Linux) or on a lab server everyone signs in to, phones included.

My promise: BioManager stays free and open source. MIT licence, no paid tier, no subscription, and your records stay on your own computer or server. Every sheet exports to Excel.

For the next three weeks I'll post one feature a day. If your lab tries it, I'd love to hear what's missing.

{site}

posts.linkedin:
The hardest part of any new lab software is the first day: moving years of spreadsheets in.

BioManager's Import from Excel takes the workbook you already keep, as it is. Columns are matched by meaning, not just by name: DOB and Born are the date of birth, Cage # is the cage, Supplier is the vendor. Each match says why it was made, and you can change any of them. Dates in any style, Male/m/♂ and your lab's own statuses are tidied. A column BioManager doesn't have becomes a new column, or goes into the notes, so nothing is lost.

You see a preview first, with every row that would be skipped and why, by its row number in Excel. The import is one batch, so it can be undone.

It works on every database: mice, fish, plasmids, vials, any organism and every inventory. Free and open source: {site}

The thing a spreadsheet can't do: connect your records.

In BioManager, a liver or serum sample in Samples links back to the mouse it came from, and one click opens that mouse in the colony. In the lab notebook, writing @mouse 16 in a qPCR page turns into a link: point at it and you see the mouse's genotype, cage and owner; click it and its record opens. The same works for plasmids, orders and every inventory.

So the question "which animal was this from?" always has an answer.

Free and open source: {site}

posts.linkedin:
What if I'm lazy but still want it to be recorded?

BioManager has no AI inside it. But if you already use an assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Cherry Studio), you can connect it to your lab. Then tell it what you did: type a sentence, or send a photo of the page in your notebook, handwriting and all.

It looks up each cage, mouse and experiment you mention, asks when something could be more than one record, and sends one proposal. In BioManager you read it in plain words, every change before and after, and press Approve. Until you do, nothing changes, and it can never delete anything or sign a page.

Free and open source: {site}

posts.linkedin:
A mouse experiment in BioManager is one page: the mice, what each got and when, and the readout.

Write the regimen once (Tamoxifen 75 mg/kg i.p. on days 1–5) and each mouse's dose is worked out from its latest weight, with the volume from the solution's concentration. The days still to do are on the calendar and the owner is reminded each morning; nothing is marked done until someone records it. Pick the reagent from your inventory and its lot is kept with the day.

The chart shows body weight (or tumour volume, a clinical score, survival) over the days, with the manipulation days marked and stars where the groups differ: Welch's t-test for two groups, one-way ANOVA for more, χ² for survival. Export gives an Excel workbook, long and wide, ready for Prism or R. On a phone, Bench mode goes one animal at a time.

Free and open source: {site}

Ordering in most labs is a shared spreadsheet plus a lot of "did anyone order the tamoxifen?".

BioManager's Orders is a board from requested to ordered to received, with vendor, catalogue number, price and grant account. An order can't be placed half filled in, and every column suggests what the lab typed before, so picking an earlier item fills the vendor, price and grant.

Protocols in BioManager's notebook have numbered versions. Start an experiment from one and its steps are copied as a checklist, with the version that was followed recorded.

Two calculations every lab repeats weekly, built into BioManager's notebook:

Plate reader: paste readings onto a 6- to 384-well heatmap, mark blanks, standards and samples, and read concentrations off the standard curve.
qPCR: paste Ct values and get ΔΔCt fold changes.
